how do i get better sleep

Here is the full picture. Sleep runs on a body clock that responds to light, so morning sunlight sets the day and dim evenings help melatonin rise. Caffeine has a half-life of about five to six hours, which means an afternoon coffee is still partly in your system at bedtime. Alcohol can make you drowsy but fragments the second half of the night, so the sleep you do get is lighter. A cool, dark and quiet room helps most people; around 18 °C is a common target. Screens matter less for the light than for the stimulation: an exciting show or a stressful email keeps the mind busy. A short wind-down routine of the same few steps each night tells your brain that sleep is coming. If you can't sleep after twenty minutes, getting up and doing something calm in dim light beats lying there frustrated. Naps are fine if they are short, under thirty minutes, and not late in the afternoon. Exercise helps sleep, but a hard workout right before bed can keep some people wired. Consistency is the biggest lever: the same wake-up time every day, weekends included, anchors everything else.
